info.description:
The JSON API a browser and an automation client both drive (JD-016).

Every endpoint lives under /api. Authenticate either with the session
cookie POST /api/auth/login sets, or with a bearer token created by
`jaildeck token add <name>`. The Authorization header takes precedence
over the cookie, and a bad token returns 401 rather than falling back to
one, so a token client fails cleanly even while a session is active.

Swagger 2.0 cannot describe a cookie as a security scheme, so only the
bearer token appears below. The cookie works on every endpoint the token
does.

The version here is the API's and is bumped with the changelog at
release time; it is not read from the binary.
info.title: Jail Deck API

get.description:
Redirects to /api/jails, so a client that guessed the base path lands on
something rather than a 404. It is behind authentication like everything
else here, so an unauthenticated caller gets 401 instead of the redirect.

What Jail Deck did: timestamp, operation, target, the command it ran, exit
code and whether it timed out (JD-011). Filters combine, and all of them
are applied to the whole file rather than to the page.

The log lives in /var/log and is rotated by newsyslog, so after a rotation
this sees only the current file. History appears to truncate with nothing
in the response to say so: that is the accepted cost of treating a log as
a log.

400.description: A filter that cannot be parsed

post.description:
Sets an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite=Strict session cookie. Secure means a
browser discards it over plain HTTP on a non-loopback origin, so reach a
remote host through an SSH forward rather than binding it to 0.0.0.0 (JD-002).

Clears the cookie and forgets the session server-side. Harmless without
one, so a client that has already lost its cookie can still call it.

get.description:
Says whether this request arrived as a session or a token, and when a
session expires. Sessions live in memory, so restarting the service signs
every browser out; tokens are stored and survive.

401.description: Neither a session nor a token

get.description:
What the firewall is doing, read-only (JD-020, JD-034). Nothing reachable from
this API can change PF.

**`state` is `not_loaded`, `disabled` or `enabled`, and none of them is an
error.** Not loaded is the common case: the reference hosts do not load PF, and
that answer is a `200` with nothing else in it. **Disabled with rules** is a
policy that is loaded and not being applied — the rules read exactly as they
would if they were, which is why `state` is the field to look at first.

`for_seconds` is pfctl's own count: the time since PF was last enabled or
disabled — **or since boot when neither has happened**. A PF loaded and never
enabled reports the host's uptime as its time disabled.

`rules` and `nat` are separate because `pfctl` keeps them separate: `-s rules`
does not show a single NAT rule. An anchor's own rules are not in the main
listing either — the main ruleset shows `anchor "jaildeck/*" all` — so every
anchor is listed in `anchors` with its rules and NAT. An anchor that could not
be read carries an `error` and the rest of the report stands.

**A rule's `text` is pfctl's own rendering**, normalised by pfctl and not
re-parsed. Only what has to be a number is taken out of it: `number` (the `@N`
that pflog refers to), the counters, `last_active`, `label`, and the first word
as `action`.

**Tables carry no address count.** `pfctl -s Tables -vv` reports one, and on
15.1 it is wrong — `Addresses: 1` for a table holding three. The count is the
length of `GET /api/firewall/tables/{name}`.

`notices` are anything pfctl printed to stderr while succeeding, other than the
ALTQ notice it prints on every verbose call.
get.summary: PF's state, rules, NAT, anchors and tables

500.description: PF is loaded and could not be read

501.description: This Jail Deck has no host access wired

get.description:
`tcpdump -n -e -tttt -r <pflog_logfile>`, the last `lines` of it (100 by default,
1000 at most).

**The file lags the packets.** pflogd buffers and flushes every
`flush_delay_seconds` — 60 unless `pflog_flags` sets `-d` — and Jail Deck does
not signal it to flush sooner: that would be acting on a daemon it does not own
(JD-034). **`log` records the packet that creates a state**, not every packet,
so a rule whose counters say thousands may have one line here.

A line is always in `raw`. Where it has the measured shape it is also taken
apart: `rule_number` is the main-ruleset number, which is unambiguous;
`anchor` is only the **last component** of an anchor's name, because that is all
tcpdump prints — `jaildeck/web` logs as `web`.

`found: false` means there is no file: nothing has been logged, or pflogd is not
running. **`truncated: true` comes with no lines**: the log was too large to
read to its end, and the lines that were read are the oldest, not the most
recent.

500.description: The log could not be read

501.description: This Jail Deck has no host access wired

`pfctl -t <name> -T show`. The name must be one `GET /api/firewall` lists;
any other is a `404` decided before PF is asked. Read when a table is opened
rather than with the report, because a blocklist table can hold a hundred

409.description: PF is not loaded

get.description:
Whether <pool>/jails and its media, templates and containers children
exist and where they are mounted (JD-006, JD-021). Read-only.

put.description:
Idempotent: creates only what is absent and reports what it made. It
refuses when a dataset on another pool is already mounted where a missing
one would go, because creating it would mount over that pool and over any
jails inside it (JD-021).

409.description: Something else is mounted there

get.description:
Every check this host must pass before it can run jails, each pass, fail
or unknown with what was observed and the remedy. Nothing here writes: a
check that cannot observe reports unknown rather than failing the request.

Running jails from jls merged with configured ones from jail.conf and
jail.conf.d, so a stopped jail is listed too — seeing it is how you start
it (JD-004).

Each jail carries its ZFS storage: datasets mounted at its path or under
it, and the user properties of its own dataset. Sizes are bytes, not the
1.41G zfs prints, so they can be compared and totalled.

Each dataset also carries the native properties it sets **locally**, out of
the four an existing dataset may be given (JD-023) — as the strings zfs
prints, so `refquota` reads `2G` rather than a byte count, and a client can
send the same value back. One a dataset merely *inherits* is absent: that
value is the parent's, and writing it here would create a local override
instead of changing what is in effect.

Both keys are absent for a jail with no dataset — and also when the pool
could not be read, which is logged at WARN rather than failing the
request, so an unreadable pool never costs you the list (JD-022).

post.description:
Clones a ready template's snapshot into the jail's own dataset, writes
its stanza to /etc/jail.conf.d/<name>.conf, optionally adds it to
rc.conf's jail_list, and starts it (JD-007, JD-030).

**The start is confirmed, not assumed.** `service jail start` exits 0
whether or not the jail came up, so the jail is read back from jls before
this reports it running.

**If a step fails, nothing is undone.** The response names the step and
says what exists — a dataset that was cloned stays cloned, a stanza that
was written stays written. Rolling back automatically is a second
destructive operation run at the moment least is known about the state.

The template is the full dataset@snapshot of a template that is ready;
GET /api/templates lists them with the snapshot each one offers. The
jail's root is cloned into <pool>/jails/containers/<name>, in the
template's own pool, because a clone cannot cross one.

Network modes: `alias` (one address on a host interface, needs ip4 and
interface), `inherit` (the host's addresses and its stack), `disable`
(no network, the default), and `vnet`.

**`vnet`** gives the jail its own network stack on an epair, with the host
end on `bridge` — which must already exist, because **Jail Deck never
creates a bridge** (JD-017); `GET /api/host` reports the ones that do.
`private: true` makes the host end a private bridge member. Measured: two
**private** members cannot reach each other at layer 2, but a private
member still reaches non-private ones and the bridge itself — so the
isolation only holds where every jail on the bridge asks for it.
`ip4` and `gateway`
are set inside the jail and are both optional — a VNET jail may instead
get its address from DHCP of its own.

The epair is created in `exec.prestart` and destroyed in `exec.poststop`,
so the jail gets the same network started from a shell as from here. The
unit is chosen when the stanza is written, from what no interface uses and
no jail configuration claims.

**A VNET jail reports no `ip` in the listing.** It sets no `ip4.addr`, so
neither `jls` nor its configuration carries one — the address is in the
jail's own stack. This response carries the one that was asked for.

If the start of a VNET jail cannot be confirmed, Jail Deck destroys the
epair, because `jail(8)` does not run `exec.poststop` for a start that
failed and the orphan would block every retry (JD-030). That is the only
thing a failed create undoes. If the cleanup itself fails, the interface
is named in the error rather than left silent.

**`limits`** are rctl rules — `memoryuse`, `vmemoryuse`, `maxproc`,
`openfiles`, `pcpu` — plus a `cpuset`. They are applied by the stanza's
`exec.poststart` and removed by its `exec.prestop`, so a jail started
from a shell is limited the same way, and a jail whose limits cannot be
applied does not start at all: `jail(8)` destroys a jail whose poststart
fails (JD-018). Sizes take a K, M, G or T suffix; `pcpu` is percent of
one core.

rctl rules need `kern.racct.enable=1`, which `GET /api/host/readiness`
reports; a spec asking for them on a host without it is refused rather
than built. `cpuset` needs no accounting and is allowed either way.

**rctl rules are keyed to the jail's name, not to the jail**, and outlive
it. A create is refused when rules are still keyed to the name it was
given — otherwise the new jail would silently run under them — and the
refusal lists them and the one command that clears them. A start that
could not be confirmed has whatever rules it managed to apply taken back
here, and says so in `rules_removed`.

**`params`** are jail(8) parameters, and only these:
`devfs_ruleset`, `securelevel` (-1..3), `enforce_statfs` (0..2),
`children.max` (0 only), `sysvmsg`, `sysvsem`, `sysvshm`
(`"disable"` or `"new"`), `allow.chflags` and `allow.set_hostname`.
Anything else is refused with the parameter named — an allowlist, because
a denylist fails open the day jail(8) gains a parameter (JD-018).

`devfs_ruleset` is checked against the rulesets the kernel has loaded.
Measured on 15.1-RELEASE-p5: a number it does not have gives the jail the
host's **whole /dev** — disks, mem, kmem, bpf — silently, while `jls`
reports the number that was asked for. Rulesets live in
/etc/devfs.rules and are yours; Jail Deck never writes them.

**`datasets`** are child datasets made beneath the jail's own, one level
down, before the stanza is written and long before the jail starts — a
jail whose `/etc/rc` expects its data mounted should find it there, and a
quota that arrives after the first write was not in force when it
mattered. Each carries native ZFS properties from JD-023's allowlist:
`mountpoint`, `refquota`, `recordsize`, `compression`, `atime`. A quota
belongs on a child rather than on the jail's root, because a clone's
`referenced` space includes the template's blocks (JD-007).

`mountpoint` is a path on the **host** and defaults to the one the child
inherits — `<jail path>/<name>`, which is `/<name>` seen from inside the
jail. A dataset wanted at `/var/db/postgres` inside a jail at
`/usr/local/jails/containers/db1` asks for
`/usr/local/jails/containers/db1/var/db/postgres`.

**A mountpoint outside the jail is refused.** Measured: ZFS makes such a
dataset without complaint, the jail cannot see it, and `zfs destroy -r`
on the jail destroys it anyway — so the jail's destroy would take a
dataset living elsewhere on the host. Data meant to outlive the jail goes
through `POST /api/jails/{name}/datasets/{child}/retain` instead.

**`properties`** are ZFS user properties set on the jail's own dataset —
the tags a client finds its jails by. They are merged, never replaced, so
a tag another tool set is left alone (JD-004, JD-023).

409.description: A jail of that name already exists, its configuration file does, rctl rules are still keyed to the name, or a child dataset is somewhere else

500.description: A step failed; the body says which and what exists

501.description: This Jail Deck has no storage wired

get.description:
The same shape as an element of the listing, storage included. It reads
that same merged listing rather than asking for a single jail, because a
jail present only in jls or only in configuration must still be found.

put.description:
The same spec as POST /api/jails, by the verb an automation client
wants: absent → created, `201`; already what the spec describes →
`200` with `changed: false`; there but different → `409` with the
differences. **Nothing is ever reconciled** — a jail that differs is
left exactly as it is and the client decides (JD-016).

Safe to repeat. A client that lost its answer to a timeout sends the
same request again and the reply says where it stands, derived from the
host rather than from anything Jail Deck remembers (JD-011).

**How "matching" is decided.** Jail Deck renders the stanza this spec
would write — against the path the jail's dataset reports and the epair
its existing stanza already claims — and compares it with the stanza on
disk, setting by setting. So the comparison covers every field the
generator writes, including ones added after this endpoint was built.
Comments, blank lines, line order and the quoting of a value are not
differences; anything else is, including a setting only one side has.

`template` and `autostart` are not in that file and are read where they
live: the root's clone origin, and rc.conf's `jail_list`. A jail whose
root was re-cloned reports the template it actually came from.

**Child datasets and tags** are compared against ZFS. A child the spec
asks for and the jail does not have is a difference, and so is one the
jail has and the spec does not name — a child takes space and `zfs
destroy -r` on the jail takes it along, so it is part of the jail in a
way a tag is not. Only direct children: the spec describes one level, so
a deeper dataset is one it could neither ask for nor disown.

Properties are compared as a subset, both kinds. A native property a
dataset sets and the spec does not mention is not a difference, because
the write side applies rather than replaces; nor is a user property
another tool set, because the write side merges (JD-023). Values compare
as text, so a `refquota` written `2048M` against one ZFS prints as `2G`
reads as a difference — parsing a size here would be the second opinion
JD-023 refuses to add.

**`start` is not compared.** It says whether to start the jail once it
has been configured, which is an instruction about the create rather
than a property of the jail — comparing it would make a jail stopped for
maintenance refuse every PUT, and acting on it would be the
reconciliation this endpoint refuses to do. The response says whether
the jail is running and the client decides.

`field` in a difference is the jail.conf(5) setting, because that is
where the difference is and what an operator would edit; the ones that
live elsewhere are named for the spec field — `template`, `autostart`,
`datasets.<child>[.<property>]` and `properties.<tag>`. They are reported
in that order: template, the configuration's settings as they sort,
datasets, tags, autostart.

The body may leave `name` out — the URL has already said it. A body that
names a different jail is refused.
put.summary: Create a jail if it is not there (idempotent)

200.description: Already what the spec describes; nothing changed

400.description: A malformed spec, or one naming a different jail

409.description: It is there and different; `differences` says how

500.description: A step of the create failed; the body says which and what exists

501.description: This Jail Deck cannot read a jail back

delete.description:
Stops the jail, takes it out of rc.conf's `jail_list`, deletes
/etc/jail.conf.d/<name>.conf, and destroys its dataset — in that order
(JD-030).

A VNET jail's epair goes when it stops, through its own `exec.poststop`.
One left behind by an earlier failed start is destroyed here too, and
named in `epair` — otherwise it would outlive the jail it belongs to.

**rctl rules are cleared on the same terms**, and named in `rules`. A
jail stopped cleanly has had them removed by its own `exec.prestop`, so
normally there are none; one left behind matters more than a stranded
interface, because rules are keyed to the name and the next jail called
this would inherit them (JD-018). Neither sweep can fail the destroy:
what could not be cleared is reported in `epair_error` or `rules_error`.
A sweep that removed something, or failed to, is audited as
`remove-leftover-epair` or `remove-leftover-rctl`.

**Child datasets go with it** (JD-007). They are listed in `taken`. A
dataset worth keeping has to stop being a child first: `POST
/api/jails/{name}/datasets/{child}/retain` moves it out.

**Snapshots, clones and holds refuse the destroy**, with each one named
and nothing touched. Each was kept on purpose, so each goes first — and
`zfs destroy -R` is never passed, which is what would make this check
decorative.

**The last word is ZFS's.** Nothing here re-checks that the jail is down
before destroying its dataset: `zfs destroy` refuses one whose jail is
running with `pool or dataset is busy`, and a check of our own would read
the state and then act on what it read, while the mount is held the whole
time. Only one of those can lose a race.

A jail with no file of its own in jail.conf.d is refused: its block is in
/etc/jail.conf, which belongs to you and which Jail Deck never writes, so
destroying the dataset would leave the jail declared and pointing nowhere.

**If a step fails, nothing is undone.** The body names the step and says
what was already done — a stopped jail stays stopped.

404.description: No such jail, or it has no dataset of its own

409.description: Snapshots, clones or holds are in the way, or the jail is configured in /etc/jail.conf

500.description: A step failed; the body says which and what was done

501.description: This Jail Deck has no storage wired

get.description:
Upgrades to a WebSocket attached to `jexec -l <name> /bin/sh -l` on a PTY
(JD-042). **Binary frames** carry the terminal's bytes, both ways. **Text frames**
carry JSON: `{"type":"resize","cols":120,"rows":40}` from the client, and
`{"type":"closed","reason":"..."}` from the server just before it closes.

`cols` and `rows` in the query are the terminal's size to start with (80×24 if
absent). The session ends when the client goes, the shell exits, the jail
stops, the login that opened it expires or is revoked, or nothing has been
typed for the idle timeout (`JAILDECK_CONSOLE_IDLE`); the closing reason is one
of `client`, `shell-exited`, `jail-stopped`, `session-expired`, `idle`.
Stopping, restarting or destroying the jail hangs its consoles up first, so the
stop does not wait on them. When the service itself stops, its shells get the
kernel's hang-up and end, with no `console-close` entry.

Audited as `console-open` and `console-close`, with who opened it, how long it
lasted and why it ended. **Nothing typed or printed is recorded.** The
`Origin` must be this host's. A browser authenticates with its session cookie;
an API token works for clients that can send the header.
get.summary: A shell in a jail, over a WebSocket

400.description: Not a WebSocket request, or a size out of range

409.description: The jail is not running

put.description:
201 when it was created, 200 when it was already there, 409 when it
exists at a different mountpoint. Idempotent, so a client that timed out
repeats the call and the answer says where it stands (JD-016).

Five native properties may be set — mountpoint, refquota, recordsize,
compression, atime — out of the sixty-odd ZFS calls editable. Anything
else is 400 naming the list: sharenfs would export the jail's data and
canmount would stop it mounting. quota is deliberately absent, because
JD-007 puts the limit on refquota.

mountpoint may be set only at creation; asking for one an existing dataset
does not have is a 409 with both values rather than a move (JD-023).

Values are not validated here. zfs answers recordsize=7K with "must be
power of 2 from 512B to 16M", and that sentence comes back — as a 400, so
a client does not retry a value that can never work.
put.summary: Create or update a child dataset

400.description: A property outside the allowlist, or a value zfs refused

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

409.description: It exists at a different mountpoint

patch.description:
The same as tagging the jail, on a dataset beneath its own.

Worth keeping separate: a jail's listing reports its own dataset's
properties, never a child's. Tag a child with otter:instance and it will
not appear on the jail — by design, or one jail with three children would
look like four instances to a client searching by tag (JD-022).

parameters.name: properties

post.description:
The same three commands in the other direction.

It need not be the jail it left, and it need not keep the name it left
with: a dataset retained from ottermq can come back as ottermq-2's data,
which is the point of keeping it. Its properties and snapshots travel with
it, because they belong to the dataset and not to where it sits.

from is the short name from GET /retained, not the full dataset path.

parameters.description: The name it will have in this jail
parameters.name: child

parameters.description: Which retained dataset to bring back
parameters.name: source

409.description: The jail already has a child of that name

post.description:
Moves it to <pool>/jails/retained/<name>. zfs destroy -r on a jail takes
its children and their snapshots with it (JD-007), so a dataset worth
keeping has to stop being a child first.

Three audited commands: zfs rename -u, zfs unmount, zfs mount. The -u is
not optional — a plain zfs rename unmounts and remounts inside the same
command, which on a running jail is the filesystem vanishing from under a
live process (JD-025).

It still unmounts: remounted=true means the filesystem moved and a running
jail just lost that path, so stop it first. Leaving the move half done is
worse — a dataset still mounted inside a jail makes the jail undestroyable.

The retained parent is created on demand and is deliberately not part of
the layout readiness check (JD-021).

parameters.description: The name it will have under retained
parameters.name: target

409.description: That retained name is taken

No -r, no children. Use it when the thing worth snapshotting is the data
and not the userland: a jail's root is a clone of a template and can be
made again, which is the premise of JD-007.

delete.description:
As above, on one dataset only. Same clone and hold refusals, same
full-name confirm.

The route that matters for a jail whose state lives in a child: rolling
the data back without touching the userland.

parameters.name: destroy_newer

post.description:
Runs `argv` inside the jail as root and returns its stdout, stderr and
exit code. This is JD-007's "hand off to in-jail provisioning" made
callable, and it is root in the jail — no more than this API already
implies (JD-001, JD-016).

**A non-zero exit is still a `200`.** The exec succeeded; the thing it ran
failed, and `exit_code` is the answer. A client that reads the HTTP status
instead is reading the wrong field. `exit_code` is `-1` when the command
never ran or was stopped by the timeout.

**`argv` is an array and there is no shell.** Nothing splits a string here,
so a quote or a semicolon in an argument is just a character. A caller who
wants a shell asks for one — `["sh", "-c", "…"]` — and has chosen it. There
is no stdin: a command that needs input writes a file in the jail first.

**The environment is clean.** The command runs under `jexec -l`, which gives
it `HOME`, `PATH`, `SHELL`, `USER` and `LANG` and nothing of the host's —
measured, plain `jexec` hands the jail everything the Jail Deck process was
started with, `jaildeck.env` included. `env` adds variables on top of that.

A request that sets `env` and whose `argv[0]` contains an `=` is refused:
`env(1)` has no way to end its assignments — measured, `env -- cmd` fails —
so it would read that argument as one more and run nothing.

**`timeout`** is a duration like `"30s"` or `"2m"`, 60s by default and five
minutes at most (JD-014). Longer is refused rather than clamped, because a
command silently given less time than asked for looks like one that failed.
Work that needs longer belongs in a template, which is prepared in the
background and polled (JD-008). A timed-out command is **killed inside the
jail**, along with anything it forked, and whatever it printed first is
still returned with `timed_out: true`.

Each stream is capped at 1 MiB and says so with `stdout_truncated` /
`stderr_truncated` — output that stops exactly at the cap is otherwise
indistinguishable from output that happened to end there.

Every call is audited with the command line it became, which includes any
environment values: a secret passed this way is written to the audit log,
which is `0700` and root-owned for that kind of reason.
post.summary: Run a command in a jail

400.description: No argv, a timeout past the cap, or a bad env name

409.description: The jail is not running

500.description: The command could not be run at all

501.description: This Jail Deck cannot run commands in a jail

patch.description:
Sets ZFS user properties on the jail's own dataset — the tags the listing
reads back (JD-004). Returns what the dataset carries afterwards, read
from ZFS rather than assumed.

PATCH, not PUT: these merge. A replacing write would strip a tag another
tool had set, and zrepl:placeholder and com.sun:auto-snapshot both live in
this namespace on real hosts.

A null value removes the property via zfs inherit, which is not the same
as setting it empty. Only user properties — the name must contain a colon
— and the value is passed through untouched (JD-011).

parameters.name: properties

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

post.description:
The upgrade path for a jail whose state lives in a child dataset: stop,
move the children aside, park the old root, clone the new one, move the
children back, start (JD-007, JD-026).

**Nothing is destroyed.** The old root is renamed to
<pool>/jails/retained/<jail>-root-<snapshot>, so a re-clone onto a bad
template costs one call to undo rather than a restore from backup. It is a
clone, so it occupies only what the jail wrote since it was made.

The jail is stopped and started again by this call, and ends in the state
it was found in. A jail that was already stopped stays stopped.

**If a step fails, nothing is retried and nothing is undone.** The response
names the step and lists every dataset that is no longer under the jail,
with where it now sits, so it can be restored with the call you already
have. Running a recovery automatically while the first failure is still
unexplained is how a bad situation becomes an unreadable one.

The template must be the full dataset@snapshot. There is no default:
every jail on a real host is already a clone of templates/<release>@base,
so defaulting to it would be a no-op dressed as an upgrade.
post.summary: Re-clone a jail's root from a template snapshot

parameters.description: The template snapshot to clone from
parameters.name: template

400.description: Missing confirm, or a malformed snapshot name

404.description: No such jail, no such template snapshot, or the jail is not on ZFS

500.description: A step failed; the body says which and where the datasets are

post.description:
Runs service jail restart.
A client disconnecting does not abort the operation: the command is
detached from request cancellation and still bounded by its own timeout
(JD-014). Audited either way.

504.description: Timed out and may still be running

get.description:
The jail's own dataset and its children's, oldest first.

Ordered by create_txg, ZFS's transaction group, not by created. A
timestamp has second granularity and two snapshots taken in the same
second tie on it — and "which is newer" is exactly what decides what a
rollback destroys. The transaction group never ties.

name is the full dataset@snapshot, which is what confirm must equal
elsewhere; short is the part after the @, which goes in a URL.

Unfiltered. On a host running zrepl this is long — one jail on the
deployment target has 39 snapshots, 35 of them hourly.

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

put.description:
201 when taken, 200 with existed=true when it was already there, so the
retry after a timeout does not raise zfs's "dataset already exists".

The jail route is recursive: zfs snapshot -r takes the jail's dataset
and every child at ONE point in time, which is what lets a root be
re-cloned while its data stays consistent with it (JD-007, JD-024).

parameters.description: Snapshot name, the part after the @
parameters.name: snapshot

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

delete.description:
Recursive, matching what the recursive create made.

409 with a dependent clone or a hold, naming them. Both are checked by
asking ZFS first — zfs get clones and zfs holds — rather than by running
the destroy and reading its complaint, so the refusal happens before
anything destructive does. Neither can be overridden here: getting past a
clone needs zfs destroy -R, which takes the clone with it (JD-024).

confirm must be the snapshot's FULL dataset@snapshot, not the word in the
path, so a script looping over jails with one snapshot name in a variable
cannot confirm every one of them by accident (JD-016).

409.description: A clone or a hold is in the way

post.description:
NEVER recursive. zfs rollback has no way to descend into children, and its
own -r means something else entirely — "destroy the snapshots newer than
this one". So this rolls back the jail's own dataset and leaves its
children where they are; a child is rolled back through its own route, as
a separate decision (JD-024).

409 when newer snapshots exist, naming every one it would destroy. Pass
destroy_newer=true to accept losing exactly those — the refusal comes
first so the second call is informed rather than a retry with more force.

Still 409, even with destroy_newer=true, when one of those newer snapshots
is held or has a clone.

parameters.description: Accept losing the snapshots taken after it
parameters.name: destroy_newer

409.description: Newer snapshots, a clone or a hold

post.description:
Turns a jail you configured by hand into a template every later jail is
cloned from — the FreeBSD Handbook's "Cloning a Jail as a Template" (17.4.3),
made callable (JD-027).

This is the general way to fill a template: it captures whatever you did to
the jail, not only packages. Installing packages into a template without a
jail is `PUT /api/templates/{name}`, which is faster and narrower.

Four commands: snapshot the jail's dataset as `@base`, clone it into
`<pool>/jails/templates/<name>`, then **promote** the clone.

The promote matters more than it looks. Without it the template is a clone
*of* the jail, and that jail can never be destroyed — `zfs destroy` answers
`filesystem has dependent clones` and names the template. After it the jail
is a clone of the template instead, which is the right way round: a template
should outlive the jail it came from, and the lineage then reads
release template → this one → the jail.

**The jail must be stopped.** A snapshot of a running jail succeeds but is an
image of a system caught mid-stride; the Handbook says to stop it first, and
taking a service down is your call rather than this endpoint's.
post.summary: Clone this jail as a template

404.description: No such jail, or it is not on ZFS

409.description: The jail is running, or that template exists

get.description:
Load average, CPU, memory and pools for the host, and CPU, memory and a
process count for every jail that is **running** — a stopped jail has no
usage to read (JD-031).

One request, because the dashboard is one page. It costs one `rctl -u` per
running jail: there is no form that answers for every subject at once.
That is also why usage is not part of `GET /api/jails` — a listing is what
an operator opens to start a jail, and it should not pay for the page that
watches them.

**`cpu.percent` is absent on the first call after a restart.** `kern.cp_time`
is cumulative and there is no kernel-maintained utilisation figure, so a
percentage exists only between two readings. The raw `cpu.ticks` are always
there, and `cpu.over_seconds` says how long the interval behind the
percentage actually was — so a reading five seconds after the last one and
one five minutes after are told apart rather than read as the same word.

A jail's `source` is `rctl` where `kern.racct.enable` is on and `ps` where
it is not. Measured on three jails: the `ps` resident sums land within 1% of
rctl's `memoryuse` and the process counts are identical, because racct's
`memoryuse` **is** the sum of the same per-process resident sizes. `rctl`
additionally answers `vmemoryuse`, `openfiles` and `cputime`; `ps` does not,
which is what `source` is for.

`pcpu` is percent of **one core**, so a jail using two whole cores reads 200.

Memory is a breakdown rather than one "used" figure: on a ZFS host most of
`wired` is the ARC, which is reclaimable, and a single number would read as
pressure that is not there.

`disks` is every physical device that answers, pooled or not — a spare or a
scratch disk can fail too. It is **empty rather than an error** on a host
without `smartmontools`, which is a package and not part of the base system,
and a disk that cannot be read never fails the rest of the report (JD-032).

**`passed` is the drive's own overall assessment, not a summary of
`failing`.** The two routinely disagree: a drive can report `PASSED` while an
attribute has been below threshold for days. `failing` is what smartctl says
is below threshold now and `failed` what it says ever was — its judgment,
carried as given rather than re-derived from `value` against `threshold`.
An attribute's `raw` is the **string** smartctl printed, never a number to
reason about: vendors pack several fields into that integer.

`device` is the name the kernel and ZFS use. Where smartctl needs a different
path for the same drive — an NVMe is `nda0` everywhere but `/dev/nvme0` to
smartctl, which refuses `/dev/nda0` — `smart_path` says so. An NVMe carries
an `nvme` block instead of an attribute table, because it has none.

Self-test logs are **read, never started**: a long test costs hours of real
I/O and choosing when to pay that is an operator's decision.

**Nothing is stored.** There is no history and no sampler; a chart over time
is Prometheus's job (JD-011).

500.description: The host could not be read

501.description: This Jail Deck has no host access wired

get.description:
The network a node's guests get unless asked otherwise (#118, JD-040): a
vm-bhyve switch with **private** ports, so guests reach the host and the
outside and not each other, the host's address on it as their gateway, and
outbound NAT through a PF anchor whose rules Jail Deck writes.

Every part is read off the host on every request (JD-011), with its
`owner`. Jail Deck's parts are put in place by `PUT /api/networks/default`:
the switch, its address and private ports, IP forwarding now and at boot,
the anchor file, and loading it. The operator's are PF itself and the three
lines `pf.conf` includes once; a failing one carries the exact `remedy`.

`usable` is a guest reaching the host; `ready` is every part, NAT included.

409.description: vm-bhyve is not ready

put.description:
Idempotent: only what is missing is done, each step audited, in order:
`create-vm-switch`, `set-vm-switch-address`, `set-vm-switch-private`,
`enable-ip-forwarding` (`sysctl`), `enable-ip-forwarding-at-boot`
(`sysrc gateway_enable=YES`), `write-pf-anchor`, and `load-pf-anchor` when PF is
up (validated with `pfctl -n` first; a file it refuses changes nothing).
`done` names what this request did; the answer is the network afterwards.

**It refuses rather than clobbers:** a switch of that name that is not a
standard one, or whose address is not `JAILDECK_VM_ADDRESS`, is a `409`
before anything runs. It never enables PF or edits `pf.conf` (JD-020):
those parts stay failing until the operator does them, with their remedy.

The same as `jaildeck init vm-network`.
put.summary: Set up the default VM network

409.description: A switch of that name is not Jail Deck's to change, or vm-bhyve is not ready

500.description: A step failed; done names those before it

get.description:
Everything under <pool>/jails/retained, with the short name a restore
asks for. Without this a client that retained something has no way to find
it again, and the whole point of retaining is that the jail it belonged to
is gone (JD-025).

Empty on a host that has never retained anything, rather than an error:
the retained dataset is created on demand.

Every template under <pool>/jails/templates, with whether it is usable and
what it was derived from.

Nothing here is stored (JD-011). `ready` is whether the `@base` snapshot
exists, which is what makes a template usable (JD-007), and `parent` is read
back from `zfs get origin` rather than recorded — so a derived template
cannot disagree with where it actually came from.

A template that exists and is **not** ready is a derive that failed part
way through. It needs no cleanup to be truthful: it is simply unusable, and
says so.

The same fields as the listing, plus **what depends on it**: every jail
cloned from it and every template derived from it, and any holds on its
snapshots.

Those are computed already — `DELETE` refuses on them — but until now a
client could only learn them by attempting a destroy and reading the 409.
That makes "can I remove this?" a question you ask by trying. Here it is a
question you ask by looking.

Both lists are present and empty rather than null, so a client rendering
them does not have to check first.

put.description:
A release template plus packages, re-snapshotted — a PostgreSQL template,
say, so every postgres jail starts with it installed (#7, JD-027).

Three steps: clone the parent's `@base`, `pkg -c <root> install -y` the
packages, snapshot the result as `@base`.

`pkg -c` chroots, so nothing is started: no jail, no stanza, no networking
for a temporary jail. It is the same shape as JD-007's `freebsd-update -b`,
which already runs against an unbooted template root.

**It installs packages and nothing else.** For anything further — `sysrc`, a
configuration file, an `initdb` — configure a jail and clone it with
`POST /api/jails/{name}/template` instead (JD-027).

**201** built · **200** it was already there and ready, so a client that
timed out can repeat the call (JD-016).

**409 if it exists but is not ready.** That is what a previous failed
derive leaves behind, and finishing it silently would install packages on
top of whatever that attempt left. Destroy it or inspect it first.

### Or prepare a release from the mirror

Send `release` instead of `from` and this builds a release template rather
than deriving one: fetch that release's `base.txz` from
download.freebsd.org into `media/`, verified against the release's own
MANIFEST. An empty `release` with no `from` means the host's own, which is
also the ceiling — a jail's userland must be the same as or older than the
kernel it runs under.

**That one answers 202 and does not wait** (JD-008). It is minutes of work;
the response says what state the template is in and the client watches the
template itself. There is no job and no job id — `GET /templates/{name}`
carries a `state` read off the filesystem and a `running` step held in
memory. **200** instead when it was already ready, which is the same
idempotent answer a derive gives.

Naming both `from` and `release` is a 400: they are two ways to build a
template, and picking one for the caller would be guessing.

A package name beginning with a dash is refused: `pkg` would read it as an
option rather than a package, and `install -y -f` is not the command that
was asked for. No shell is involved either way.

If `pkg` fails, the clone stays **without** its `@base` and the listing
reports it as not ready. pkg's own message comes back, as a `400` when pkg
ran and refused — a package that does not exist is the request's fault.

202.description: Preparing a release; watch the template

400.description: A bad name, or a package pkg refused

409.description: It exists but is not ready, or the parent is not

delete.description:
Destroys the template dataset and its snapshots.

**409 while anything is cloned from it**, naming every one. A template's
snapshot is the origin of every jail made from it, so destroying it would
take them with it. ZFS would refuse too — but only after being asked, with
a message about dependent clones rather than a list of the jails running on
them. This asks first, so the refusal is an answer.

A jail that should outlive its template is not stuck: `zfs promote` on the
jail moves the dependency the other way, exactly as cloning a jail as a
template does in reverse (JD-027).

`confirm` is the template's name. Unlike a snapshot's, it is unambiguous on
its own — a template name is unique within the pool, where `nightly` names a
snapshot on every dataset that has one.

Never `zfs destroy -R`: that would take the dependent clones this refuses to
touch, which would make the check decorative.

409.description: Something is cloned from it

get.description:
Image templates for VMs (JD-037): a cloud image's disk in a zvol under
`.images` in vm-bhyve's default datastore, sealed with an `@base` snapshot
that guests' disks are cloned from.

Nothing is stored (JD-011). `state` is `ready` when `@base` exists and
`written` when the zvol does and `@base` does not, which is a write that
stopped. `fetching` and `writing` are this process's work in flight, with
`running` saying which step (JD-008). `source` and `sha512` are user
properties on the zvol: what it was written from, and the checksum of the
exact archive. `guests` are the guests cloned from it.

`sources` is what can be prepared, with whether its verified archive is
already on the host. When vm-bhyve is not ready, or its datastore is not on
ZFS, the answer is a 200 that says so in `vm_bhyve` and `problem`, with no
images.

The same fields as the listing. An image being fetched has no zvol yet and
is still here, with its `running` step: the resource a client was told to
watch exists from the moment the work starts (JD-008).

put.description:
Three stages, each audited (JD-037):

1. **fetch-image**: the source's archive and the publisher's checksum file.
The archive is downloaded as `.part` and renamed only once its SHA-512
matches, so an archive under its own name is a verified one. Skipped when
the source's archive is already there.
2. **write-image**: a sparse zvol the size of the disk in the archive, with
`volmode=dev` so the host never reads the guest's partition table, and the
disk written straight into it by `tar -xO`.
3. **seal-image**: the `@base` snapshot, which makes it ready.

**202 and no waiting** (JD-008): minutes of work, and the client watches
`GET /vm-images/{name}`. **200** when it was already ready, so a client that
timed out can ask again.

The body may be empty: the source is then the image's own name, so
`PUT /vm-images/debian-13` prepares Debian 13.

**409** when the image exists and is not ready (a write that stopped:
remove it and prepare it again; the archive is kept), was written from
another source, is already being prepared, or when vm-bhyve or its
datastore cannot hold images.

400.description: A bad name, or not a source

409.description: Not ready, another source, busy, or no store

delete.description:
Destroys the zvol and its `@base`. The archive stays: it belongs to the
source, and preparing the image again starts at the write.

**409 while any guest's disk is cloned from it**, naming the guests. ZFS
would refuse too, in terms of datasets. `confirm` is the image's name.

409.description: Guests use it, or it is being prepared

get.description:
`vm list`, read on every request (JD-019, JD-035).

**`vm_bhyve` is `ready`, `not_installed` or `not_configured`, and none of them is
an error.** Not configured carries vm-bhyve's own words in `problem` — the same
ones Host Setup reports, with the remedy beside them there.

`state` is vm-bhyve's: `running` and `bootloader` carry the `pid` of the bhyve
or loader process; `stopped`; `suspended`, a guest stopped with its state saved;
`locked`, marked running by the host in `locked_by`, in a datastore shared
between hosts. **Read on every request and never stored** (JD-011).

`cpu` and `memory` are the guest's configuration as written (`"2"`, `"512M"`),
not re-parsed. `autostart` is whether the guest is in `rc.conf`'s `vm_list`, and
`autostart_order` its place there.

`switches` are vm-bhyve's virtual switches, which a created guest's NIC can be
on (JD-038): read when vm-bhyve is ready, and empty otherwise.

500.description: vm-bhyve answered and could not be read

501.description: This Jail Deck has no host access wired

post.description:
A guest from a VM image template (JD-037, JD-038), in five audited steps:

1. **vm-create**: `vm create` from Jail Deck's own template (UEFI, one virtio
disk, no NIC) with `cpu`, `memory` and a cloud-init seed: `ssh_keys` for the
image's default user, the guest's name as its hostname, and `network` as a
static address when given (DHCP otherwise).
2. **vm-pin-cpus**, when `cpuset` is given: vCPU i pinned to host CPU
`cpuset[i]`, written as `bhyve_options="-p 0:<cpu> ..."` (JD-041). One host
CPU per vCPU, each a different one, and each one the host has: bhyve aborts
on a CPU it lacks only at start, while `vm start` still exits 0 — measured.
3. **vm-add-network**: one NIC on `switch`, when given, with the MAC the seed
matches it by. **The switch must exist**: vm-bhyve accepts one that does not,
and the guest then boots with a NIC attached to nothing — measured.
4. **vm-replace-disk**: the disk vm create made is replaced by a clone of the
image's `@base` at `disk`, `volmode=dev`. The guest grows its own root
filesystem into it on first boot.
5. **vm-start**, when `start` is true, confirmed as `POST /vms/{name}/start` is.

Everything is checked first: the name, sizes, keys, addresses, that the image
is ready, that `disk` is at least its size, that the name is free and the
switch exists. **A step that fails after the guest exists destroys it again**,
and the error names the step. A start that fails leaves the guest, which is
whole, and says so.

Measured on isengard: created in 3 seconds, and reachable over SSH on its static
address 18 seconds after it started.

400.description: A value refused, an image or switch that does not exist, a disk smaller than its image

409.description: The name is taken, the image is not ready, or vm-bhyve is not

500.description: A step failed; the guest was destroyed again

get.description:
The guest's row from `GET /api/vms`, and what `vm info <name>` adds. The name
must be one the listing has; any other is a `404`, and one vm-bhyve could never
have created is a `400`.

`memory_resident` and `consoles` exist only while the guest's bhyve instance
does. A console is the host's end of a null-modem pair (`/dev/nmdm-<name>.1B`).
A network's `device` is the tap of the current run — a new one on every start —
and `size` and `used` are bytes.
get.summary: One guest: its row, consoles, network interfaces and disks

404.description: vm-bhyve has no guest by that name

409.description: vm-bhyve is not installed or not configured

500.description: vm-bhyve answered and could not be read

501.description: This Jail Deck has no host access wired

put.description:
The idempotent form of `POST /vms` (JD-016, JD-041), with the same body. A
guest vm-bhyve does not have is created, as `POST` creates it: `201`. One it
has is compared against the request: `200` when it is what the request
describes, and **`409` with `differences` when it is not — and it is left
exactly as it is.** Nothing here reconciles a guest towards a request.

What a guest was made with is read off the host, not from a record: its
vm-bhyve configuration (cpu, memory, the pin in `bhyve_options`, each NIC's
switch), its cloud-init seed (address, gateway, nameservers, SSH keys) and
disk0's clone origin and size. Defaults resolve as a create resolves them, so
a request that leaves `cpu`, `memory` or `disk` out matches the guest those
defaults made.

**`start` is not compared.** It is an instruction about the create, not a
property of the guest: a guest stopped for maintenance would otherwise refuse
every `PUT`. The answer carries the guest's state, and the client decides.

A guest outside vm-bhyve's default datastore, or with no cloud-init seed, was
not made by Jail Deck from an image, and is refused with `409`: there is
nothing to compare. The body may leave `name` out; one naming another guest is
refused.

200.description: Already what the request describes; nothing changed

400.description: A value refused, or a body naming another guest

409.description: There and different; `differences` says how. Or not one Jail Deck made

500.description: A step of the create failed; the guest was destroyed again

delete.description:
`vm destroy -f`: the guest's dataset, the disk cloned from its image with it, and
its configuration (JD-038). The image is then free to be removed, if nothing
else uses it.

**A running guest is refused**, as vm-bhyve refuses it: stopping is its own
decision, with its own deadline (`POST /vms/{name}/stop`). `confirm` is the
guest's name.

409.description: Running, in its boot loader, or locked by another host

get.description:
Upgrades to a WebSocket attached to the guest's first console port: the host's
end of its nmdm pair, as `vm info` names it, made raw before anything passes
(JD-042). Frames as for a jail's console: binary for the terminal's bytes, text
for JSON control. A serial line has no size, so `resize` changes nothing; the
guest's own `stty` or `resize` does.

**One session per guest**: a second is refused with `409`. An outside
`vm console` or `cu` on the host can still attach at the same time; FreeBSD lets
root past an exclusive lock, measured. **Closing the console does not log anyone
out of the guest**: a login on the serial line stays logged in.

The session ends as a jail's does, and also with `guest-stopped` when the guest
is no longer running (looked at every 5 s: a powered-off guest gives the device's
reader nothing at all), or `console-closed` when the device ends. Audited as
`console-open` and `console-close`; nothing typed or printed is recorded.
get.summary: A guest's serial console, over a WebSocket

409.description: The guest is not running, or a console is open on it already

post.description:
Stop, as `POST /vms/{name}/stop` does it — powering off a guest that does not
answer within 60 seconds, and saying `forced: true` — then start. A stopped guest
is only started. Not vm-bhyve's own restart, which asks the guest to reboot and
has no deadline (JD-036).

404.description: vm-bhyve has no guest by that name

409.description: Locked, in its boot loader, or vm-bhyve not ready

500.description: vm-bhyve refused, or the guest did not stop or start

504.description: Timed out and may not have completed

post.description:
`vm start <name>`, detached from Jail Deck so that nothing that happens to the
command can reach the guest, and then confirmed: vm-bhyve has to list it as
`running` within 15 seconds (JD-036). A guest already running, or in its boot
loader, is answered as it is and nothing runs. Audited as `vm-start`.

A client disconnecting does not abort it.

404.description: vm-bhyve has no guest by that name

409.description: Locked by another host, or vm-bhyve not ready

500.description: vm-bhyve refused, or the guest did not come up

504.description: Timed out and may not have completed

post.description:
`vm stop <name>` — the ACPI power button — and then up to 60 seconds for vm-bhyve
to list the guest as `stopped`. **A guest that has not stopped by then is powered
off** with `vm poweroff -f`, the equivalent of pulling the plug, and the answer
says `forced: true` (JD-019, JD-036). A guest whose operating system is still
booting ignores the power button, so stopping one straight after starting it ends
that way.

A stopped or suspended guest is answered as it is. One in its boot loader is a
`409`: vm-bhyve asks on a terminal before killing a loader, and Jail Deck has none.
Audited as `vm-stop`, and `vm-poweroff` when it came to that.
post.summary: Stop a guest, powering it off if it does not answer

404.description: vm-bhyve has no guest by that name

409.description: Locked, in its boot loader, or vm-bhyve not ready

500.description: vm-bhyve refused, or the guest did not stop

504.description: Timed out and may not have completed

principal.description:
The three a session carries, which a command does not (JD-042): who
opened it ("session", or "token:<name>"), how long it lasted, and why it
ended. Omitted on every other entry.

request_id.description:
RequestID is the caller's X-Request-Id, omitted when it sent none
(JD-011: nothing is stored that the request did not supply).

error.description:
Error says this one anchor could not be read -- it was listed and then
gone, most likely. The rest of the report still stands.

rule.description:
Rule is as tcpdump printed it: 2/0, or 5.web.1/0 for a rule inside an
anchor. RuleNumber is the main-ruleset number before the first dot or
slash, which is unambiguous; Anchor is only the anchor's last name
component, which is not (JD-034).

flush_delay_seconds.description:
FlushDelaySeconds is how far behind the packets the file may be.
pflogd buffers, and Jail Deck does not signal it to flush (JD-034).

truncated.description:
Truncated means the log could not be read to its end, and so no lines
are given: the ones that were read are the oldest, not the most recent.

for_seconds.description:
ForSeconds is pfctl's own "Enabled for 4 days 17:02:03", in seconds:
the time since PF was last enabled or disabled -- or since boot, when
neither has happened. Measured: a PF loaded and never enabled reports
the host's uptime as "Disabled for", which is not how long it has been
disabled in any sense an operator means (JD-034). Absent when not loaded.

notices.description:
Notices are anything pfctl printed to stderr while succeeding, other
than the ALTQ notice every -v call prints. Reported rather than
swallowed, and rather than failing the page over.

rules.description:
Rules is the main filter ruleset. NAT is separate because pfctl keeps
it separate: -s rules does not show a single NAT rule (JD-034).

action.description:
Action is the first word -- pass, block, match, anchor, nat, rdr -- for
the interface to colour by, and nothing cleverer.

last_active.description: LastActive is pfctl's timestamp as printed, absent where it says N/A.

number.description:
Number is the @N from -vv. pflog names a rule by it and nothing else
prints it, which is why the ruleset is read with -vv at all.

flags.description: Flags is the column as pfctl printed it, -pa-r-- and the like.

observed.description:
Observed is what the host actually said, empty when nothing could be
observed.

remedy.description:
Remedy is set on every failed check and only there: a command for a
root shell where one exists, otherwise the file or setting to change.

mountpoint_taken_by.description:
MountpointTakenBy is set on a missing dataset when another dataset, on
any pool, already has its expected mountpoint. Ensure refuses then.

guests.description:
Guests are the guests whose disk is a clone of @base. An image is not
removed while there are any.

name.description: Name is the zvol's last component, which is what a client uses.

ready.description:
Ready is whether @base exists. An image is usable only then, and one
whose write stopped part way is a zvol that is not ready.

sha512.description:
SHA512 is the checksum of the archive the disk was written from. The
source's "latest" moves; this names the exact build.

size.description:
Size is the zvol's volsize: the image's disk, and the smallest disk a
guest cloned from it can have.

source.description:
Source is the catalog entry the image was written from. Empty for a
zvol under .images that Jail Deck did not write.

state.description:
State is read off the disk except for the -ing forms, which come from
what this process is doing (JD-008).

used.description:
Used is what the image costs the pool. Sparse and compressed, so far
less than Size.

dataset.description:
Dataset is where images are kept: .images under vm-bhyve's default
datastore.

problem.description: Problem is why images cannot be prepared here, when they cannot.

vm_bhyve.description:
VMBhyve is the same answer GET /api/vms gives: ready, not_installed or
not_configured. Images live in vm-bhyve's datastore.

source.description:
Source is what is being prepared, so an image with no zvol yet can
still say what it will be.

fetched.description:
Fetched is whether the verified archive is already on the host, so
preparing an image from it starts at the write.

url.description: URL is the archive's, for the operator to see what will be fetched.

source.description:
Source is the catalog entry to prepare the image from. Empty means the
image's own name, when that is a source.

name.description:
Name is the dataset's own name, directly beneath the jail's: "data"
becomes <pool>/jails/containers/<jail>/data. One level at a time, as
the dataset endpoints take it.

properties.description:
Properties are native ZFS properties, from the allowlist in JD-023:
mountpoint, refquota, recordsize, compression, atime. The same map the
PUT /api/jails/{name}/datasets/{child} body carries, so a dataset is
described the same way wherever it is asked for.

mountpoint is a path on the *host*, and defaults to the one the child
inherits -- <jail path>/<name>, which is /<name> seen from inside the
jail. A dataset meant at /var/db/postgres inside a jail at
/usr/local/jails/containers/db1 asks for
/usr/local/jails/containers/db1/var/db/postgres.

config.description: Config is the file the stanza was written to.

datasets.description:
Datasets is what each child dataset the spec asked for came to --
created now, or already there and brought to its properties. The same
report PUT /api/jails/{name}/datasets/{child} gives for one of them.

epair.description:
Epair is the host end of a VNET jail's epair -- what appears on the
bridge, and what a failed start would leave behind. Empty for every
other mode.

epair_removed.description:
EpairRemoved says the epair was destroyed after a start that could not
be confirmed. Only Jail Deck will do that: jail(8) does not run
exec.poststop for a start that failed (JD-030).

error.description:
Error is why it stopped. The body of a failed create carries both: what
exists is the recovery information, and this is the reason it is
needed. Filled in by the handler, which is where the response is
decided -- the service returns a Go error like every other method here.

failed_at.description: FailedAt names the step that stopped, and is absent on success.

from.description: From is the template snapshot the root was cloned from.

properties.description:
Properties are the jail dataset's user properties as they stand
afterwards, read back rather than assumed (JD-023).

root.description:
Root is the jail's own dataset and Mountpoint is where it is mounted,
which is the jail's path.

rules_error.description:
RulesError says why they could not be taken back. The next create of
this name will refuse until they are gone, and say so.

rules_removed.description:
RulesRemoved are the rctl rules taken back after a start that could
not be confirmed. A start that fails part way through exec.poststart
keeps the rules it had already added and never runs exec.prestop, so
they would otherwise outlive the jail they are named after (JD-018).

properties.description:
Properties are the native ZFS properties this dataset sets locally, out
of the four an existing one may be given (JD-023). Absent rather than
empty when it sets none, and a property it merely inherits is not here:
that value belongs to the parent, and setting it here would create a
local override rather than change what is in effect.

The jail's *user* properties stay at the jail level, where JD-004 put
them -- a client tags the jail, not each of its datasets.

used.description:
Bytes, not the "1.41G" zfs list prints by default, so a client can
compare and total them.

conflict.description:
Conflict is set when the dataset exists somewhere other than where the
request said. Mountpoint is settable only at creation (JD-023), so this
is not a change the API will make -- and reporting both values says more
than refusing would.

remounted.description:
Remounted says whether the filesystem was actually carried to the new
mountpoint. False when the dataset was not mounted to begin with --
which is not a failure, just nothing to carry.

blocked.description:
Blocked is set when something kept on purpose is in the way. Nothing
ran: the jail is still there, still configured, still as it was.

config.description: Config is the configuration file that was deleted.

epair.description:
Epair is the interface destroyed with the jail. Normally there is
none: a VNET jail's exec.poststop takes its own epair away when it
stops. One turns up here when an earlier start failed and left the
epair behind, which would otherwise outlive the jail (JD-030).

epair_error.description:
EpairError says why a leftover epair could not be removed. The destroy
carried on regardless -- the jail and its dataset are the point, and a
stranded interface is a nuisance rather than a blocker. It is named
here because a silent one is an interface on a bridge that nothing
will ever account for.

failed_at.description: FailedAt names the step that stopped, and Error says why.

root.description:
Root is the jail's own dataset, named even when the destroy was
refused -- it is the dataset an operator would go and look at.

rules.description:
Rules are the rctl rules cleared with the jail. Like the epair there
are normally none: a jail stopped cleanly has had them removed by its
own exec.prestop. One turns up here when an earlier start failed
(JD-018).

rules_error.description:
RulesError says why they could not be cleared, on the same terms as
EpairError -- except that a leftover rule is worse than a stranded
interface, because the next jail of this name would inherit it.

stopped.description: Stopped says the jail was running and this stopped it.

taken.description:
Taken are the child datasets destroyed along with the root. A jail's
children go with it (JD-007), and they go silently unless listed here.

unlisted.description: Unlisted says it was taken out of rc.conf's jail_list.

changed.description:
Changed says whether this call changed anything on the host. It is
false for a jail that already matched and false for one that differs:
nothing here reconciles a jail towards a spec (JD-016).

config.description: Config is the file the stanza was written to.

datasets.description:
Datasets is what each child dataset the spec asked for came to --
created now, or already there and brought to its properties. The same
report PUT /api/jails/{name}/datasets/{child} gives for one of them.

differences.description:
Differences is every setting the spec and the host disagree about,
and is the whole of the answer when they do.

argv.description:
Argv is the command and its arguments. An array, never a string:
there is no shell here to split it, and nothing for a quote or a
semicolon in an argument to mean. A caller who wants a shell asks for
one -- ["sh", "-c", "..."] -- and has chosen it deliberately.

env.description:
Env are variables for the command, on top of the clean login
environment jexec -l gives it. The host's own environment is never
passed in: measured, jexec hands the jail everything the Jail Deck
process was started with, jaildeck.env included (JD-016).

timeout.description:
Timeout is a Go duration: "30s", "2m". Absent means 60s; longer than
five minutes is refused rather than clamped, because silently running
for less time than asked is how a caller concludes their command
failed when it was cut off.

argv.description:
Argv as it was asked for, so a caller reading a log sees what it sent
rather than the jexec line it became.

exit_code.description:
ExitCode is the command's own. **A non-zero one is still a 200**: the
exec succeeded and the thing it ran failed, and that distinction is
the whole point of this endpoint (JD-016). It is -1 when the command
never ran or was stopped by the timeout.

stdout_truncated.description:
Set when a stream was cut off at the cap. Reported rather than left to
be inferred from a length, because output ending exactly at the cap is
indistinguishable from output that happened to end there.

timed_out.description:
TimedOut says the command was stopped rather than finished. The
process was killed inside the jail -- jexec does not fork, so the
process is the command -- along with anything it had forked.

datasets.description:
Datasets and Properties are filled by the listing and by GET
/api/jails/{name}, and left out everywhere else. omitempty rather than an
empty collection on purpose: a start or restart response reports what the
operation knew, and claiming "datasets: []" there would say the jail has
none when the truth is that nothing looked.

cpuset.description:
CPUSet is the cpu list the jail is pinned to: "0-3", "0-3,8", "2". It
is not an rctl rule and needs no accounting, so it is the one limit a
host with kern.racct.enable=0 can still have.

memoryuse.description:
MemoryUse is resident memory and VMemoryUse is address space. Both are
a byte count with an optional K, M, G or T suffix, in either case --
what rctl(8) accepts, measured.

pcpu.description:
PCPU is percent of one core: 100 is a whole core, and a sixteen-core
host takes up to 1600. How many the host has is the host's to judge,
and it refuses more than it has (JD-012).

bridge.description:
Bridge is the bridge the host end of the epair joins, and is required
for NetworkVNET. **It is the operator's.** Jail Deck adds and removes
its own epairs and nothing else: it never creates a bridge, never adds
a physical interface to one, and never edits rc.conf's network
settings (JD-017). GET /api/host reports which bridges exist.

gateway.description:
Gateway is the jail's default route, set inside the jail. Only
meaningful with IP4, because a route needs an address to leave by.

interface.description:
Interface is the host interface the alias is added to. NetworkAlias
only: a VNET jail reaches the network through Bridge instead.

ip4.description:
IP4 is the address, with its prefix: 192.0.2.10/24. Read by
NetworkAlias, where it is required, and by NetworkVNET, where it is
optional -- a VNET jail may get its address from DHCP inside itself.

private.description:
Private makes the host end a private member of the bridge.

Measured on 15.1-RELEASE-p5: two private members cannot reach each
other, but a private member still reaches non-private members and the
bridge itself. So this isolates a jail from the other jails that also
ask for it -- not from every jail on the bridge, and not from the
host. Worth being exact about, because the weaker guarantee is the one
an operator would assume they had.

old_root.description:
OldRoot is where the previous root is parked. A re-clone destroys
nothing (JD-026).

parked.description:
FailedAt and Parked are the recovery information: which step failed, and
where every dataset that is no longer under the jail currently sits.

running.description:
Running is the jail's state afterwards, which is the state it was found
in unless a step failed before it could be started again.

create_txg.description:
CreateTXG is ZFS's transaction group: the only exact ordering. Two
snapshots taken in the same second share a Created, so a client deciding
which is newer has to compare this instead.

name.description:
Name is "dataset@snapshot" as zfs prints it, and is what confirm= must
equal on a destroy or a rollback (JD-024).

short.description: Short is the part after the @, which is what the URL carries.

autostart.description:
Autostart adds the jail to rc.conf's jail_list, which is what makes it
come back after a reboot and nothing else (JD-030).

datasets.description:
Datasets are child datasets created beneath the jail's own, in the
order given, before the jail is configured or started (JD-007).

hostname.description:
Hostname defaults to the jail's name, which is what an operator writing
the stanza by hand almost always sets it to.

limits.description:
Limits are rctl rules and a cpuset, applied by the generated stanza
when the jail starts (JD-018).

params.description:
Params are jail(8) parameters, and only ones on the allowlist: the
API refuses anything else, naming it. The values are whatever
jail(8) wants -- a number for devfs_ruleset, a word for sysvshm, a
flag for allow.chflags -- so the map is typed by the allowlist
rather than by Go (JD-018).

properties.description:
Properties are ZFS user properties set on the jail's own dataset --
the tags an automation client finds its jails by, which Jail Deck
carries and never interprets (JD-004, JD-023).

start.description:
Start says whether to start the jail once it is configured. A pointer
because absent means yes: creating a jail and leaving it down is the
unusual request, and it should be the one that has to be spelled out.

template.description:
Template is the snapshot the jail's root is cloned from, in full:
<dataset>@<snapshot>. There is no default, for the reason JD-026 gives
for a re-clone — every jail is a clone of some template, so a default
would be a choice made silently.

raw.description:
Raw is the string smartctl printed, never a number to reason about.
Seagate encodes several fields into one integer -- ada3's
Raw_Read_Error_Rate reads 200021688 and is not a count of anything.

over_seconds.description:
OverSeconds is how long that interval was, so a reading taken five
seconds after the last one and one taken five minutes after are told
apart rather than read as the same word.

percent.description:
Percent is busy time as a share of the interval since the last
reading. Absent on the first call after a restart -- there is nothing
to measure against, and zero would be a lie (JD-031).

ticks_per_second.description:
TicksPerSecond is what a tick above is worth -- kern.clockrate's
stathz, which on this host is 127 while hz is 1000. Reported because
handing out cumulative counters without saying what they count invites
every consumer to make the same wrong guess (JD-033). Absent when the
rate could not be read, which costs the seconds and nothing else.

device.description: Device is the name the host uses -- ada3, nda0, da0.

failing.description:
Failing are the attributes smartctl says are below threshold now, and
Failed those it says were at some point. Its judgment, reported as
given rather than re-derived from value against threshold.

kind.description:
Kind is "ata" or "nvme", and says which of the two halves below to
expect.

nvme.description: NVMe carries what an NVMe says instead of an attribute table.

passed.description:
Passed is the drive's **own** overall assessment. It is not a summary
of the attributes below and routinely disagrees with them: isengard's
ada3 reports true while attribute 184 has been failing for days
(JD-032).

pool.description:
Pool is the pool this disk is part of, empty when none is. The join
neither tool does alone: smartctl cannot say which pool a failing
disk holds up, and zpool status cannot say the disk is failing.

rotation_rate.description: RotationRate is 0 for an SSD and absent where the drive does not say.

self_test.description:
SelfTest is the most recent self-test the drive logged. Read, never
started: a long test costs hours of real I/O and choosing when to pay
that is an operator's decision (JD-032).

serial.description:
Serial is reported because the question after "which disk is failing"
is "which one do I unplug", and on a four-disk box that otherwise
means powering down to read labels.

smart_path.description:
SmartPath is the device path smartctl had to be given, present only
when it is not /dev/<Device>. An NVMe is nda0 to ZFS and to the kernel
but can only be read as /dev/nvme0 -- smartctl refuses /dev/nda0 -- so
an operator told "nda0 is failing" who reaches for smartctl would
otherwise be refused with a message about namespace ids (JD-032).

vdev.description:
Vdev is the name the pool knows it by -- gpt/backup1, ada0p4 -- which
is what `zpool status` prints and therefore what an operator reading
that output is looking for.

error.description:
Error says this one jail could not be read. The rest of the report is
still worth having, so a jail that fails is reported rather than
failing the request.

pcpu.description:
PCPU is percent of one core, so a jail using two whole cores reads
200. From racct, which maintains it as a decaying average, or summed
from ps.

vmemoryuse.description: rctl answers these and ps does not.

configured.description:
Configured is how many jails the host has in total, running or not,
so the dashboard can say "3 of 5" without a second request.

disks.description:
Disks is every physical device that answers, pooled or not. Empty on
a host without smartmontools, which is a package rather than base
(JD-032).

disks_unavailable.description:
DisksUnavailable says why Disks is empty when it is not because the
host has none: smartctl not installed, not on the service's PATH, or
refusing to list devices. JD-032 promised a host without disk health
would say why; until this field it only said nothing (#95).

hours.description:
Hours is the drive's power-on hour count when the test ran, which is
how a self-test log dates itself.

egress.description: Egress is the interface NAT sends the guests out of.

gateway.description: Gateway is Address without its prefix: what a guest is given.

ready.description: Ready is whether every part passes, NAT included.

switch.description:
Switch is the vm-bhyve switch it is, and Address the host's address
on it, which is the guests' gateway.

usable.description:
Usable is whether a guest on the switch reaches the host and no other
guest: the switch, its address and its private ports are in place.

note.description:
Note is said when something done takes effect later: a switch made
private applies to guests as they next start.

ready.description: Ready is whether every part passes, NAT included.

switch.description:
Switch is the vm-bhyve switch it is, and Address the host's address
on it, which is the guests' gateway.

usable.description:
Usable is whether a guest on the switch reaches the host and no other
guest: the switch, its address and its private ports are in place.

remedy.description:
Remedy is set on a part that fails and is the operator's: what to
change, as precisely as it can be said. Jail Deck's own parts are put
in place by PUT /api/networks/default instead.

clones.description:
Clones are datasets made from one of this template's snapshots -- every
jail cloned from it, and every template derived from it.

mountpoint.description: Mountpoint is where pkg -c operates and where a jail's clone comes from.

name.description:
Name is the last component of the dataset, which is what a client uses:
"15.1-RELEASE", "postgres-16".

parent.description:
Parent is the template this one was derived from, empty for a release
template built from base.txz. Read from the clone's origin rather than
recorded: a derived template cannot outlive or disagree with its parent.

ready.description:
Ready is whether the @base snapshot exists. A template is usable only
then (JD-007), and a derive that failed part way through is a template
that exists and is not ready.

referenced.description:
Referenced is the whole userland; for a derived template most of it is
still shared with its parent, so Used is what the packages cost.

running.description:
Running is the step executing right now, absent when nothing is. Held in
memory and never written down: a restart kills the work, so a marker
that survived it would be claiming something false.

snapshot.description:
Snapshot is the full dataset@base once it exists, which is what a jail
is cloned from.

state.description:
State is where this template has got to, read off the filesystem except
for the -ing forms, which come from what this process is doing (JD-008).
A template that has only been fetched has no dataset and still has a
state, because the resource a client watches has to exist from the
moment the work starts.

blocked.description: Blocked is set when something is cloned from the template. Nothing ran.

step.description: Step is the stage in the operator's words, not a command line.
